strengths: Addresses an important gap in T2AV evaluation with a comprehensive, first-of-its-kind unified benchmark for joint audio-video generation assessment
Well-designed taxonomy-driven prompt construction (500 prompts) with semantic deduplication and video inversion ensuring broad coverage and physical plausibility grounding
Dual-level evaluation framework thoughtfully integrating objective signal metrics (DOVER++, CLAP, DeSync) with subjective MLLM-as-judge assessments featuring reasoning-first protocol
Rigorous empirical evaluation of 11 representative models (proprietary, open-source, and pipelines) with per-dimension analysis revealing diagnostic failure modes
Valuable diagnostic finding: 'Audio Realism Bottleneck' showing even top models (Veo-3.1) score ~50/100 on audio realism vs ~87/100 on video quality
Strong dataset diversity analysis via CLIP/CLAP embeddings demonstrating superior semantic coverage compared to existing benchmarks (JavisBench, VABench)
Excellent reproducibility documentation with extensive appendices (A-G) providing experimental details, prompts, and MLLM evaluation logic
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 5-6 radar plots) that communicate model capabilities across multiple dimensions
weaknesses: Critical absence of human evaluation and correlation studies: no validation that proposed metrics correlate with human judgment, undermining confidence in the evaluation framework
MLLM reliability unanalyzed: no inter-rater agreement studies, sensitivity analysis to temperature/decoding strategy, or empirical characterization of MLLM biases on T2AV content
Objective metrics not validated for generative content: DOVER++, LAION-Aesthetic, and CLAP trained on natural/UGC data; unclear if they appropriately measure AI-generated audio-video quality
No comparison between objective vs. subjective metric rankings: critical gap for validating the dual-level framework's design choices and internal consistency
Restricted scope: limited to 4–10 second videos (acknowledged), primarily English prompts, and no support for long-tail physical interactions or multimodal scenarios
Primarily engineering contribution: most metrics are existing tools (DOVER++, CLAP, DeSync); MLLM-as-judge is standard practice; main novelty is integration rather than methodological innovation
Dataset and code release status unclear: 'practical and evolving foundation' lacks specificity; no discussion of long-term maintenance strategy or saturation risk with only 500 prompts
Incomplete analysis of key findings: paper identifies audio realism bottleneck but provides limited investigation of root causes or actionable insights for model improvement
Statistical rigor gaps: no confidence intervals, significance tests, ablation studies, or sensitivity analyses on metric choices (e.g., 2 FPS frame sampling)

Reproducibility concerns: heavy reliance on proprietary APIs (Gemini, model access); video tokenization/frame sampling details insufficient for reproduction; prompts examples anecdotal rather than systematic

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark construction with principled taxonomy-driven pipeline ensuring semantic diversity and physical plausibility across 500 prompts aggregated from multiple high-quality sources

Dual-level evaluation framework combining extensive objective metrics (video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment) with novel MLLM-as-a-judge subjective evaluation addressing limitations of single-modality metrics

Extensive empirical evaluation of 15 representative T2AV systems with systematic failure mode analysis, difficulty trends, and diagnostic insights (e.g., Audio-Visual Realism Disconnect, dynamics bottleneck)
Exceptional transparency and reproducibility with detailed appendices covering all prompts, evaluation procedures, MLLM protocols, and ground-truth data; promised public dataset release
Significant practical contributions identifying specific bottlenecks (audio realism, fine-grained synchronization, instruction following) that guide future research and model development
Well-structured presentation with informative visualizations, concrete qualitative examples, and clear methodology making the work accessible and actionable for the community
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in evaluation metrics—primarily combines existing metrics (DOVER-VT, CLIP, ImageBind, DeSync) without introducing fundamentally new evaluation methodologies

MLLM-as-a-judge framework shows notable limitations: human-MLLM agreement significantly lower than inter-human agreement (14.5% gap; L1=1.087 vs 0.949), severe cross-family MLLM disagreement (L1=1.322-1.476), raising questions about reliability of subjective scores

Prompt diversity concerns despite 500 prompts—acknowledged inability to capture extreme long-tail distributions, limited linguistic diversity (primarily English), unclear generalization to real-world user intents beyond taxonomy-defined coverage

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates reported; Bradley-Terry ranking lacks uncertainty quantification; limited sensitivity analysis (only 100 videos tested for metric stability)

Incomplete analysis of metric necessity and independence—while Figure 9 shows low pairwise correlations, no systematic feature selection determines which dimensions are most discriminative or necessary for differentiating models

Fixed, static benchmark with unclear mechanisms for evolution—no principled procedure for incorporating new prompts while maintaining taxonomy balance, limited scalability of expensive MLLM evaluation, risk of obsolescence as field advances
Evaluation of proprietary systems (Sora, OpenAI) cannot be independently verified; API restrictions and potential version staleness limit reproducibility for key commercial models

Potential evaluation biases not thoroughly explored—checklist emphasis on cinematic realism may favor certain models, MLLM inherent preferences not analyzed, no discussion of cultural/gender biases in 500 prompts
